newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Samsung's AST in build-to-order plans.
newsitem.headline: Samsung's AST in build-to-order plans.

text.p: AST Research Inc, part of South Korea's Samsung Electronics Co, is joining the ranks of personal computer makers adopting the build-to-order manufacturing method to be more efficient, company officials said on Tuesday.

"Every country (in the Far East) will have its FCTP (final configuration, testing and packaging) site very soon, otherwise we cannot be competitive," Hoon Choo, president of AST Research (Far East) Ltd told Reuters.
Computer makers who have adopted different forms of build-to-order methods include Compaq, Dell Computer and Apple Computer Inc.
U.S-based AST has merged with Samsung Electronics, becoming its wholly-owned subsidiary.
"We are working with many partners on how to bring down the order cycle in Southeast Asia," Sam Ghebranious, the company's Southeast Asia managing director told a news conference.
He said AST was evaluating three sites, including Singapore and Malaysia, and aimed to decide on one by late 1997 or early 1998, to do final product configuration for Southeast Asia.
Now, AST's plant in China is working with basic modules and adding on the final configurations according to Southeast Asia customers' requirements
The FCTP, or build-to-order model, has been implemented in Australia and Middle East, Hoon said.
The move is part of a strategy to return AST to profitability by 1999 when its revenues is expected to top US$3.0 billion, company officials said.
AST's revenue in 1995 prior to the merger transition period was US$2.4-2.5 billion, Ghebranious said.

Hoon said he expected the Far East region that covers Asia Pacific and the Middle-East to contribute 30-35 percent of AST's worldwide revenue by the turn of the century, up from about 20 percent currently.
Hoon said the new method would be applied to desktop products, low-end servers and notebooks.
Ghebranious said AST had new products to roll out all the way to the third quarter of 1998.
These includes the launch of a NetPC and new notebooks.

A NetPC works on the concept of lowering the costs of networking computers through remote maintenance. It is not stripped down like a network computer which does not have a disk drive and takes all its applications from the network.
